text: There was a man from Ramathaim-zophim, in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives; one was named Hannah, the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Year after year this man would go up from his town to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.
Whenever the day came for Elkanah to sacrifice, he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved Hannah, though the LORD had closed her womb.
Her rival taunted her bitterly, provoking her because the LORD had closed her womb.
So it went year after year: every time Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, Peninnah would provoke her, and Hannah would weep and refuse to eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why won't you eat? Why is your heart so heavy? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"
After they had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah got up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the LORD's temple.
In deep anguish Hannah prayed to the LORD, weeping bitterly.

And she made a vow: "LORD of hosts, if you will only look on the misery of your servant and remember me, if you will not forget your servant but give her a son, then I will give him to the LORD for all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever touch his head."
As she kept on praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was praying in her heart; her lips were moving, but no sound came out. So Eli thought she was drunk
and said to her, "How long will you go on drinking? Put your wine away."
"No, my lord," Hannah answered. "I am a woman in deep distress. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink; I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.
Do not take your servant for a worthless woman; it is out of my great anguish and grief that I have been speaking all this time.

versions.text: Do not take your servant for a worthless woman; I have been speaking out of great grief and sorrow."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew ends with עַד־הֵנָּה ("until now" / "all this time"), which the current rendering omits. Restoring it completes Hannah's explanation of how long she has been pleading and improves the closing rhythm of the sentence.

text: Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant what you have asked of him."
She said, "May your servant find favor in your eyes." Then she went on her way, and she ate, and her face was no longer downcast.
Early the next morning they rose and worshiped before the LORD, and then returned home to Ramah. Elkanah made love to his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In the course of time Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, "I asked the LORD for him."
When Elkanah went up with all his household to offer the yearly sacrifice to the LORD and to fulfill his vow,
Hannah did not go. She said to her husband, "Once the boy is weaned, I will take him and present him before the LORD, and he will stay there for good."

"Do what seems best to you," her husband Elkanah told her. "Stay here until you have weaned him; only may the LORD make good his word." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

When he was weaned, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh, though he was still a small child. [Footnote: Hebrew tradition reads "three bulls"; other ancient witnesses read "a three-year-old bull," which agrees with the single bull slaughtered in verse 25.]

versions.text: When he was weaned, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh, though he was still a small child.
versions.explanation: Following the Hebrew with "three bulls" is defensible, but it creates an apparent inconsistency with the singular "the bull" in verse 25. A brief footnote explaining the textual variation helps listeners and readers without altering the base text.

text: When they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli,
and she said, "Pardon me, my lord. As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this child, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him.
So now I give him to the LORD. For his whole life he will be given over to the LORD." And there he worshiped the LORD.
